newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan seen keeping money policy intact -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan seen keeping money policy intact -analysts.

text.p: The Taiwan central bank is likely to keep its long-standing monetary policy on worries that any policy shift would either chill a gathering recovery or overheat the red-hot stock market, analysts said on Tuesday.
"The central bank is in a very, very difficult position -- it can neither lower nor raise interest rates," said National Securities manager Allen Huang.
"Simply put, the central bank has no choice but to keep the monetary policy unchanged," Huang said. "Its best policy right now is to do absolutely nothing."
Speculation has centred on whether the central bank would alter its "stable to loose, but not too loose" monetary policy at its quarterly board meeting at 0700 GMT on Thursday.
Most analysts voiced doubt about a rate cut, saying this risked throwing petrol on an already-sizzling bourse.
Contrarily, an interest rate hike -- aiming to clamp down on the languid liquidity that many experts say is driving the stock index -- could hurt the island's slowly improving economy.

"There is no room for the interest rates to rise further because economic growth is so important for Taiwan," Morris Li, vice president and country treasurer at Citibank Taiwan, told Reuters Financial Television.
"The central bank cannot affront to risk jeopardising the economy by raising rates. There's no doubt the economy is the utmost concern for the central bank and government," Li said.

Some analysts said local politics coloured central bank decision-making, referring to Vice President and Premier Lien Chan's recent comment that it was healthy for the stock index to rise above 10,000 points -- as it did briefly on Tuesday.
"The central bank simply does not have the guts to tighten the monetary policy," a foreign brokerage executive said on condition of anonymity.
"The central bank will not dare challenge Lien's comment. Don't forget: The central bank is under the cabinet and any market-dampening move would be a slap in Lien's face," he said.
Lien heads the cabinet in his post as premier.
Even before Lien made the remark, central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong had said on July 16 that monetary policy was no cure-all in face of concerns of stock market overheating.
On Tuesday, the benchmark index surged to an intra-day peak of 10,057.95 but lost steam in late trade to finish at 9,892.34, down 30.71 points or 0.31 percent from Monday's close.
Analysts said a rate reduction was even more unthinkable.

Taiwan's stock market has more than doubled since mid-1996 in what brokers call a liquidity-driven, technology-focused rally -- making it one of the world's best performing markets even without further priming in the form of looser liquidity.
"Given the fact that the liquidity is fairly loose at the moment, it's impossible for the central bank to adopt a looser monetary policy," said Huang of National Securities.

Most analysts brushed away concerns that the frantic stock rally was heading toward an unsustainable bubble similar to the one that burst in 1990 when the index peaked at 12,495.34. The index freefell 80 percent over the next eight months.
"The central bank appears to be less worried about the stock market as investors are much more rational and local economy is backed by good fundamentals," Citibank's Li said.
"We are not in an economic bubble," Li said.
